Because only forbidden magic could have killed that way, Warden Morgan of the White Council threatens Harry with execution if another such death occurs and treats him as the suspect. Investigating, Harry ties the murders to a new drug that grants the Sight and to the vampire Bianca, clashes with crime lord Johnny Marcone, and discovers that the missing husband, Victor Sells, has become a dark sorcerer killing at a distance with storm-powered rituals. Victor turns demons and conjurations on Harry. In a final confrontation at Victor's lake house during a storm, Harry, aided by the reporter Susan Rodriguez, destroys Victor and his ritual, clears himself with the Council, and keeps Murphy's uneasy trust.

recaps.text: Harry Dresden, Chicago's only professional wizard, takes on two problems at once. Karrin Murphy of the police department's Special Investigations unit brings him to a grisly double murder: a mob bodyguard and a call girl killed in bed by magic that tore the hearts from their chests, a spell of terrible power and skill. That same morning a nervous woman named Monica hires Harry to find her missing husband, Victor. Harry recognizes that only forbidden black magic could have committed the killings, which puts him in immediate danger from his own kind: the White Council forbids using magic to kill, and Harry already lives under a suspended death sentence for a killing in his past. He begins pulling at both cases, not yet aware that they are the same case.

Warden Morgan of the White Council shadows Harry, promising to see him executed the instant another magical death occurs and treating Harry himself as the prime suspect. Harry's inquiries link the murders to a new street drug that grants a brief flash of magical Sight, and to the world of the vampire courts: he confronts Bianca, a Red Court vampire who runs a brothel and employed the dead woman, and the meeting ends in mutual injury and lasting enmity. Meanwhile the missing husband, Victor Sells, proves far harder to find than a runaway should be. Harry's digging draws the attention of Gentleman Johnny Marcone, Chicago's crime lord, whose own man was one of the victims; Marcone tries to buy Harry off the case, then to warn him away, and is refused.

The killer strikes again, and the spell is turned on Harry himself; only luck and quick warding save him, and Morgan's threat becomes immediate. Harry realizes the murders, the drug, and the missing man all trace back to Victor Sells, who has become a self-taught dark sorcerer working from a lake house outside the city and killing with a storm-fueled ritual that rips out hearts at a distance. Victor sends a demon and other conjured horrors after Harry to stop the investigation. Battered, hunted by his own Council, and distrusted by Murphy after he is caught withholding information, Harry races to reach Victor before the next storm gives the sorcerer the power to kill again - and before the next heart torn out is his own.

Harry and Susan drive out to the lake house as a storm gathers, where Victor is preparing a mass ritual. Susan, having secretly taken the Sight-granting drug, is overwhelmed and endangered, and Harry faces Victor amid conjured scorpions and demons with almost nothing left. Turning Victor's own storm-drawn power against him, Harry destroys the sorcerer and his ritual, ending the killings. Murphy, arriving to find the aftermath, arrests Harry briefly but comes to accept he was on her side, and their working partnership survives. The Council's death sentence is lifted for now. Harry is left exhausted, cleared, and more entangled than ever in the hidden world, having made a lasting enemy of Bianca and drawn the lasting interest of Marcone.

characters.description: A Legion Varus centurion, Galina Turov's subordinate and lover, and Etta's father. He is maintaining a false explanation for his daughter's move to Dust World while privately trying to contain the consequences of her dealings with Claver.
characters.name: James McGill

characters.description: The tribune commanding Legion Varus and McGill's superior officer and lover. At his family home, she supports the public claim that Etta went to Dust World for protection.
characters.name: Galina Turov

characters.description: McGill's underage daughter, now living on Dust World. Her family has been told that she left for safety, while McGill conceals the real circumstances of her departure and her involvement in a transaction with Claver.
characters.name: Etta

characters.description: A concealed adversary who appears near McGill's home after Etta's transaction and creates an immediate threat there.
characters.name: Claver

characters.description: The leading body in a clone network that also uses physically powerful Class Three workers. The workers remain loyal to this primary line and identify McGill by the equipment taken from its Earth body.
characters.name: Claver Prime

characters.description: The leader of the Dust World colony and operator of its clandestine revival system. He restores McGill with an illegal process that combines stored DNA and tapper memories, then requires him to keep the operation secret.
characters.name: Etta's grandfather

characters.description: A near-human Hegemony scientist whose eidetic memory may preserve the text of the destroyed book. She will reconstruct it only if Galina Turov authorizes the revival of her dead friend, whose data she has retained.
characters.name: Florimel

characters.description: A deceased enemy agent who was close to Florimel and previously killed both her and McGill. Florimel holds his preserved DNA and memories, and makes his revival the price of reproducing the destroyed book.
characters.name: Rash

characters.description: Legion Varus's senior primus and operational commander beneath Galina Turov. He briefs the legion's officers aboard their new transport as an unusually early deployment begins.
characters.name: Graves

characters.description: A legionnaire in McGill's Third Unit. She joins the unit as Legion Varus prepares for an early deployment with its destination still undisclosed.
characters.name: Kivi

characters.description: A Legion Varus veteran serving in McGill's Third Unit as the legion begins an early deployment whose purpose remains undisclosed.
characters.name: Harris

characters.description: An adjunct in Third Unit who temporarily commands it while McGill is absent. He is part of the established officer group preparing the unit for its new mission.
characters.name: Leeson

characters.description: A member of McGill's Third Unit who deploys with Legion Varus aboard its new transport.
characters.name: Carlos

characters.description: McGill's friend and a Legion Varus centurion preparing for the legion's new deployment.
characters.name: Manfred

characters.description: An experienced former centurion transferred from Legion Victrix into McGill's unit after refusing a Hegemony desk post. Visibly uneasy about joining Varus, she does not explain why Victrix removed her from combat duty.
characters.name: Former Victrix adjunct

characters.description: McGill's former partner, Etta's mother, and a native of Dust World. She confronts him over their daughter's dangerous experience there and fears Etta's continuing determination to enter legion service.
characters.name: Della

characters.description: A Third Unit specialist who openly questions McGill's training plan before a shipboard war game. His willingness to challenge the centurion marks him as an independently minded member of the unit.
characters.name: Cooper

characters.description: A senior noncommissioned weapons specialist in Third Unit. During the Green Deck exercise, he coordinates the plasma attack on an enemy tower and helps carry an overloaded weapon toward the breach.
characters.name: Sargon

characters.description: A Mogwa chief inspector who expects McGill to deliver the bioterminator text. Galina Turov identifies him as the recipient of McGill's concealed courier mission.
characters.name: Xlur

characters.description: A former Legion Varus officer now working for the Hegemony. He treats McGill as absent without leave and sends him through a gateway to Storm World.
characters.name: Winslade

characters.description: A Blood World sub-centurion who recognizes McGill's standing among his troops and escorts him to the Iron Eagles primus.
characters.name: Churn

characters.description: The hostile Blood World officer commanding the Iron Eagles position on Storm World. Although McGill recognizes him from an earlier campaign, the primus refuses to help him rejoin Legion Varus.
characters.name: Iron Eagles primus

characters.description: The officer leading Third Unit's vulnerable light platoon. She maintains a professional bearing when McGill returns from a long absence.
characters.name: Barton

characters.description: A veteran reassigned by McGill to provide experienced support for Barton's vulnerable light platoon.
characters.name: Mahler

characters.description: A Third Unit soldier preparing to transfer into bio-specialist work. She declines the opportunity to train as a stealth scout and is willing to leave Legion Varus if the new specialty does not suit her.
characters.name: Sarah

characters.description: Third Unit's leading technical specialist. During the first patrol on Storm World, she identifies the sudden growth of immense vegetation as evidence of Wur activity.
characters.name: Natasha

characters.description: A blue scupper who formally recognizes McGill as First Man after McGill defeats the natives' previous leader. He becomes McGill's deputy within the newly acquired scupper force.
characters.name: Second Man

characters.description: The former commander of Legion Germanica, now tribune of Fort Beta's Blood World legion. He is a prior opponent of McGill and an antagonistic but necessary ally as the surviving forces prepare for another Wur assault.
characters.name: Maurice Armel

characters.description: The former grand admiral of Battlefleet 921 and newly appointed Mogwa governor of the province. He arrives at Storm World to judge Earth's frontier performance and orders the human force to prove itself in the coming battle.
characters.name: Governor Sateekas

characters.description: A former adversary of McGill and Florimel who now operates Fort Beta's oversized revival machinery. He is capable of processing giant bodies and is currently Florimel's partner.
characters.name: Saurian revival technician

characters.description: The ruler of the underground scupper city. She is hosting a Rigelian negotiator, has authority over alliance terms, and agrees to arbitrate McGill's challenge under native custom.
characters.name: Native queen

characters.description: Rigel's representative in the scupper capital and a fighter McGill encountered during an earlier campaign. He seeks an alliance with the native population and accepts McGill's customary challenge before the queen.
characters.name: Squanto

characters.description: The named female Claver. Female clones are forbidden within the Claver network.
characters.name: Abigail

characters.description: A separate Claver who claims exile from the primary clone line. He says he created the female clone Abigail, is hunted by the other Clavers, and offers McGill a plan to change the battle.
characters.name: Renegade Claver

characters.description: The renegade clone who joins McGill's force and proposes destroying the final Wur nexus to remove the local Wur's command intelligence.
characters.name: Claver-X

recaps.ending: McGill destroys the final Wur nexus and dies inside it. Sarah performs an accelerated revival, and he learns that the disconnected Wur attacked both Fort Beta and their Rigelian allies. Sateekas judges the human army inferior in direct combat, but Squanto refuses to make Rigel the province's new enforcer. Earth therefore retains the position, and McGill uses the promised truce to return Squanto alive. Rigel withdraws and transmits Florimel's engram, enabling her revival. She confirms that she surrendered the genuine Mogwa-killing formula to Rigel. Legion Varus evacuates Storm World, while Maurice Armel's legion remains behind to rebuild with the scuppers. Two months later, Claver-X brings Etta home. Central and the primary Claver line are hunting him, but McGill hides their contact and kills two pursuing clones. Galina Turov resumes her relationship with McGill while warning that the Core Worlds are investigating Xlur's permadeath. The formula's spread, Claver-X's role, Florimel's plan to seek her partner's revival, and McGill's exposure remain open.
recaps.in_short: James McGill pursues Etta and a book containing a Mogwa-killing formula, survives illegal revivals, and kills Chief Inspector Xlur while hiding the formula's loss. Legion Varus deploys to Storm World against the Wur, where McGill gains command of the native scuppers. Rigel intervenes, and Governor Sateekas makes Earth's provincial status depend on the conflict. Maurice Armel betrays the garrison and helps Claver Prime trade Florimel to Rigel. A renegade Claver-X then guides McGill toward the final Wur nexus. McGill destroys it and dies, but Sarah revives him. The leaderless Wur attack both armies, and Rigel withdraws. Sateekas keeps Earth as local enforcer only because Squanto refuses the appointment. Florimel returns by transmitted engram and admits giving Rigel the genuine formula. Varus leaves, Armel remains to rebuild, and Etta later comes home with Claver-X while the formula, Xlur investigation, and clone conflict remain unresolved.

recaps.text: Previously: James McGill serves as a centurion in Legion Varus under Tribune Galina Turov, with whom he also has a personal relationship. His daughter Etta wants a military life, while her parents remain divided over the dangers surrounding her. Claver is not a single ordinary adversary but part of a clone network whose bodies and memories complicate any attempt to stop him permanently. McGill has also dealt with Florimel, a near-human Hegemony scientist, and with the Mogwa officials who oversee Earth's place in Province 921. His history includes campaigns involving Blood World forces, the Wur, Rigel, and officers such as Maurice Armel and Sateekas. These relationships leave McGill caught between family obligations, legion command, and the demands of powers that can determine humanity's status.

Etta has left for Dust World after secretly selling Claver a false copy of a valuable book. Claver confronts McGill and demands the genuine volume, which contains a formula for a genetic poison lethal to the Mogwa. McGill discovers that the real book is missing, kills one Claver body, and uses its teleport equipment to follow Etta. Two worker clones attack him on Dust World and send him to his death. Etta's grandfather restores McGill through an illegal colonial revival process and warns that exposure would endanger them all. McGill then finds Etta, who returns the real book and explains that she feared its use as a mass weapon. The colony has revived one of the worker clones as a more capable Claver. It attacks McGill and Etta, destroying the book and mortally wounding McGill before Etta kills it. McGill dies again, and the physical text appears lost.

McGill returns through another irregular revival and reports to Galina Turov. Because Central has no copy of the destroyed book, he brings her to Florimel, whose eidetic memory can reproduce it. Florimel demands the revival of her dead friend in exchange. Before that bargain is resolved, Legion Varus deploys early aboard Leggett to Storm World, an oceanic frontier planet threatened by the plantlike Wur. A separate Blood World legion accompanies it. During a shipboard exercise designed to favor the non-revivable Blood World troops, McGill forces a breach and causes permanent losses on the opposing side. Galina and Graves execute him off the record, but the death also conceals a courier mission. Florimel's encrypted message was supposed to carry the bioterminator text to Chief Inspector Xlur. McGill reveals only after dying that he deleted the message without reading it. He is now committed to meeting Xlur without the data the Mogwa official expects.

McGill revives on Mogwa Prime, where Chief Inspector Xlur expects the missing formula. Xlur is an exiled official who hopes the information will restore his political position. McGill pretends that the nonexistent file requires his personal translation, using the delay to study his confinement. When Xlur moves to kill him, McGill reverses the attack and disintegrates the inspector. He then sends Galina a false confirmation of delivery, fabricates evidence that Xlur killed himself, and takes his own life so that he can be revived elsewhere. McGill returns off-grid on Earth after four months away and learns that Leggett has already departed. A former Varus officer sends him through a gateway to Storm World. He arrives inside an isolated Blood World fort during lethal tides and storms, but its hostile primus refuses to help him reach Varus and shoots him. McGill has reached the campaign, but only through another death and another concealed chain of events.

After repeated transfers and revivals, McGill rejoins Third Unit on Storm World and restores his command. Galina confirms that she concealed his Core Worlds mission and begins limited patrols against the Wur. McGill's first patrol encounters rapidly grown forest and pod walkers. The unit defeats the attack but loses equipment and personnel. Ordered to stop a scupper war party from cutting Wur trees, McGill instead faces a series of unexplained disappearances. He, Cooper, and Kivi fall into an underground transport network created by the native scuppers. Kivi dies while testing its gravity-shifting tubes, but McGill retains the information needed for her revival. Cooper and McGill learn to navigate the system and emerge far from their unit on a coastal beach. As a major storm and tide approach, hundreds of scuppers surround them at the cliff top. McGill sends the concealed Cooper away to report and remains alone to attempt contact with the native force.

A scupper leader challenges McGill's courage. McGill defeats and spares him, and the natives recognize McGill as their new First Man. He gains roughly seven hundred fighters and a deputy called Second Man. Galina allows the scuppers into Fort Alpha, but their earlier destruction of Wur trees has already drawn a large response. During the assault, McGill arms the natives and holds the eastern gate while other sections collapse. Wur acid troops and pod walkers overrun most of the fort, leaving the remaining defenders trapped in Gold Bunker. Second Man identifies a buried entrance to the native transport tubes. McGill persuades Galina to abandon the final bunker and leads the survivors underground as the Wur break in. Sixteen humans and a much larger scupper group use the network to reach Fort Beta. Its automated defenses kill Harris before McGill destroys the weapon and secures entry. Fort Alpha has fallen, but Galina, McGill, and their remaining organized force survive at the stronger Blood World position.

At Fort Beta, Galina and Tribune Maurice Armel form an uneasy alliance. A ship belonging to Governor Sateekas arrives to judge whether Earth remains capable of enforcing order on the frontier. Galina uses the gateway network to seek reinforcements. She later commands Leggett when three Rigelian transports attack. Leggett destroys one ship and escapes the missile response by entering warp, leaving the ground force isolated. Thousands of armored Rigelian troops land inside the fort while Wur forces gather outside. McGill discovers that captured Rigelian guns and extended human force blades can defeat their resistant armor, helping Varus repel the landing at severe cost. Florimel is present with Armel's near-human troops and is now partnered with a Saurian revival technician. Before the garrison can recover, the Wur attack Fort Beta. Their pod walkers climb over wounded members of their own force to reach the battlements. By the end of the assault's opening phase, the wall defense has failed and the defenders must prepare for close combat inside the fort.

Armel commits his giant troops and personally leads a counterattack that defeats the Wur breach, though the giants suffer irreplaceable losses and Kivi is trampled. Graves then sends McGill to reconnect with the scuppers. McGill reaches their vast underground city and finds a Rigelian representative negotiating with the native queen. He challenges the Rigelian under local custom, wins the unarmed contest, and gains command of the native armies. Governor Sateekas nevertheless refuses to declare Earth victorious while Rigel and the Wur remain active. McGill returns to Fort Beta with about three thousand native volunteers and begins turning them into a disciplined force. Natasha then shows him restricted intelligence indicating that Rigelian and Wur troops are occupying the same area without fighting. Armel's guards arrest them, and Natasha is killed during the struggle. McGill reports the apparent alliance to Armel and Graves. To keep their attention and gain leverage, he falsely claims that he may have a way to communicate with the Wur.

Maurice Armel reveals that he knows about the bioterminator book and wants McGill to obtain another copy for a buyer. Convinced that the Rigel-Wur alliance has doomed the campaign, he plans to evacuate the officers and abandon the garrison. When Graves objects, Armel shoots him. Claver Prime arrives under a deal with Armel, takes McGill captive, and abducts Florimel after killing her Saurian partner. He sells Florimel to Rigel for the formula in her memory and delivers McGill to Sateekas as cover for the trade. McGill attacks Claver and tries to redirect blame for Xlur's death, but Sateekas privately reveals that he already knows McGill killed the inspector. The governor regards that death as useful. He also explains that an Imperial succession crisis has nearly destroyed his former fleet. Rigel has been offered Earth's place as provincial enforcer, and humanity will be expunged if its army loses the approaching battle. McGill returns to warn the garrison and is immediately imprisoned by Armel's troops.

As Rigelian and Wur forces march together against Fort Beta, Cooper frees McGill from the brig. McGill warns Armel, then encounters a Claver who is separate from the Prime held by Sateekas. This renegade, later called Claver-X, says he created the forbidden female clone Abigail and was exiled by the primary line. He proposes destroying the final Wur nexus, the command intelligence coordinating the planet's plant forces. McGill accepts and leads Third Unit, scuppers, and Claver-X through the mountains while the main armies assault the fort. Rigelian troops inflict heavy losses along the route, and lethal tides kill more of the expedition. McGill eventually sends the heavies back and reaches the nexus on an isolated plateau. With no explosives, he attacks it using a captured shotgun and force blades. Floodwater cuts off his escape, but he penetrates the nexus and destroys it after a drone receives his final data. McGill dies inside the structure, leaving the Wur without centralized direction.

Sarah revives McGill through an accelerated procedure. Although Fort Beta is devastated, the destruction of the nexus has driven the Wur out of control, and they attack both the defenders and their Rigelian allies. Sateekas rules that Earth was inferior in direct battle and offers its enforcer role to Rigel. Squanto refuses Imperial service, so Sateekas retains Earth instead. McGill invokes the governor's safe-passage promise to save Squanto from execution. Rigel withdraws and sends Florimel's mental engram, allowing Sarah to revive her. Florimel confirms that she gave Rigel the genuine Mogwa-killing formula. Varus evacuates, while Armel's legion remains on Storm World to rebuild with the scuppers. Two months later, Claver-X returns Etta safely to Earth. McGill kills two worker clones pursuing him and conceals the encounter from Galina. She warns that Central and the primary Claver line are hunting Claver-X, while the Core Worlds are investigating Xlur's permadeath. Etta is home and Earth retains its status, but the formula, the clone conflict, and McGill's possible exposure remain unresolved.

characters.description: A fourteen-year-old Londoner, orphaned as a baby and raised by his uncle Ian. He attends Brookland School and seems ordinary to his classmates, but a childhood of unusual holidays has left him fluent in several languages and trained in climbing, diving and karate without his ever being told why. Self-contained and stubborn, he refuses to accept the official account of his uncle's death and starts asking questions nobody wants him to ask.
characters.name: Alex Rider

characters.description: Alex's uncle and legal guardian, who took him in as an infant after his parents died. A private, undemonstrative man who worked for a bank and travelled abroad constantly, he taught Alex an odd assortment of skills and told him almost nothing about himself. His death in a car accident is the news that opens the book.
characters.name: Ian Rider

characters.description: The American housekeeper of the Rider household, in her late twenties. She came to London to study law, took a summer job looking after Alex and never left. Warm, direct and protective, she is the nearest thing Alex has to family, and her right to stay in Britain depends on the household continuing.
characters.name: Jack Starbright

characters.description: The head of the Special Operations division of MI6, which does its business behind the front of the Royal & General Bank. Grey, precise and almost entirely unreadable, he weighs people strictly by their usefulness and is untroubled by the idea of sending a schoolboy into the field.
characters.name: Alan Blunt

characters.description: Blunt's deputy at Special Operations, rarely seen without a peppermint. Her manner is gentler than her chief's and she shows flickers of conscience about what the department is doing, but she signs off on the same decisions.
characters.name: Mrs Jones

characters.description: The leader of the four-man Special Air Service unit Alex is attached to during selection training in the Brecon Beacons. Hard, disciplined and openly contemptuous of having a boy dumped on his team, he makes the fortnight as difficult for Alex as he can.
characters.name: Wolf

characters.description: MI6's gadget-maker, a large, cheerful man who takes obvious delight in his work. Because Alex must pass as an ordinary teenager, he builds his equipment into things a boy would plausibly carry, and he is one of the few people at the department who treats Alex kindly.
characters.name: Smithers

characters.description: A self-made billionaire, born in poverty in Beirut and now the owner of a computer empire based in Cornwall. His Stormbreaker machine is the most advanced computer in the world, and he is giving one to every school in Britain, a gesture that has made him a national figure. Small, watchful and charming in public, he is short-tempered with his own staff, and MI6 want to know why an agent investigating him ended up dead.
characters.name: Herod Sayle

characters.description: Sayle's butler and personal bodyguard, a former circus knife-thrower whose face was ruined in an accident with his own act. The injury has left him with a permanent rictus and speech nobody but his employer can interpret. He is still lethally accurate with a blade.
characters.name: Mr Grin

characters.description: Sayle's assistant and the manager of his plant, a brisk, humourless woman with a heavy accent who conducts Alex's tour and decides where he is and is not allowed to go.
characters.name: Nadia Vole

characters.description: A young Russian contract killer, quiet, polite and entirely without theatre, who arrives at Sayle's estate by night with cargo nobody is meant to see. He works for people whose names are never spoken and treats killing as a trade like any other.
characters.name: Yassen Gregorovich

recaps.ending: Alex reaches London aboard an aircraft and drops through the glass roof of the Science Museum, landing on the Stormbreaker display seconds before the Prime Minister can press the button that would have activated every machine in the country and released the virus into Britain's schools. The launch is stopped and the plot exposed. Sayle escapes in the confusion and is cornered on a rooftop, where he draws a gun on Alex; before he can fire he is shot dead by Yassen Gregorovich from a helicopter, silencing him on his employers' behalf. Yassen leaves Alex alive, tells him to go home, and says they will meet again. Alex learns that it was Yassen who killed Ian Rider, and that the men who supplied Sayle with the virus were never Sayle's own. MI6 thank him, return him to school, and make no promise to leave him alone; Blunt and Mrs Jones have seen how useful a fourteen-year-old agent can be. Alex goes back to Brookland with a dead uncle, a debt he cannot collect, and the knowledge that the department now regards him as an asset rather than a schoolboy.
recaps.in_short: Fourteen-year-old Alex Rider is told that his uncle and guardian, Ian Rider, has died in a car crash, and discovers instead that the wrecked car is full of bullet holes and that his uncle was a career MI6 officer. The department blackmails Alex into finishing the assignment his uncle died on: infiltrating the Cornish plant of Herod Sayle, a computer magnate about to donate a Stormbreaker machine to every school in Britain. Posing as a competition winner, Alex uncovers a shipment of sealed vials, breaks into the mine beneath the plant, and finds that the computers are being loaded with a modified smallpox virus. Sayle intends to kill the nation's schoolchildren in revenge for being humiliated as a boy by the classmate who is now Prime Minister. Alex escapes, reaches London, and drops through the roof of the Science Museum in time to stop the launch. Sayle is shot dead by the Russian assassin Yassen Gregorovich, who spares Alex and reveals that he was also the man who killed Ian Rider.

recaps.text: Fourteen-year-old Alex Rider is woken before dawn with the news that his uncle and guardian, Ian Rider, has been killed in a car accident. Ian, a banker who travelled constantly, has raised Alex since his parents died when he was a baby, with the household kept by Jack Starbright, a young American who came to London to study and stayed on. The account of the crash does not convince Alex: he is told his uncle was not wearing a seat belt, which was not like him at all. Tracking the wrecked car down to a scrapyard, Alex sees that the bodywork is punched through with bullet holes, and he is nearly killed in the car crusher when the yard's owner finds him. Following the trail to the Royal & General Bank, where Ian supposedly worked, he finds an office that is nothing like a bank and staff who are nothing like bankers.

At the Royal & General, Alex is taken in hand by Alan Blunt and Mrs Jones, who run the Special Operations division of MI6. They tell him that Ian Rider was an intelligence officer, killed while investigating Herod Sayle, a computer magnate who is about to donate one of his new Stormbreaker machines to every school in Britain. They also tell him that his uncle spent Alex's whole childhood quietly preparing him for the same work: the languages, the climbing and diving trips, the martial arts. The department wants a boy inside the Cornish plant, since a teenager can go where an agent cannot, and it makes clear that a refusal would have consequences for Jack's right to remain in the country. Alex is sent to a Special Air Service selection camp in the Brecon Beacons, where he is attached to a four-man unit whose leader, Wolf, resents him. He survives the fortnight, and the department's gadget-maker, Smithers, equips him with weapons built into ordinary teenage possessions.

Alex arrives at Sayle Enterprises in Cornwall under the name Felix Lester, supposedly the schoolboy who won a competition to test the Stormbreaker before its launch. He meets Herod Sayle, who keeps a Portuguese man-of-war in a tank in his office and tells the story of his rise from poverty in Beirut; Sayle's mute, disfigured butler, Mr Grin, a former circus knife-thrower; and Nadia Vole, the assistant who controls where Alex is allowed to go. The tour of the plant is smooth and tells him nothing. Left to himself, Alex explores the estate and the nearby town of Port Tallon, and an attempt is made on his life while he is out alone, confirming that somebody there knows exactly who he is. Every part of the site connected with the computers themselves is sealed off, and the whole operation is running to a deadline that ends with the Prime Minister switching on the network in London.

At night Alex watches a helicopter land on the estate and unload a consignment brought by a young Russian who is treated with more deference than Sayle's own staff: Yassen Gregorovich, a professional killer working for whoever is behind Sayle. Alex breaks into the disused mine workings that run beneath the plant and finds a sterile production line where the Stormbreakers are being finished. Each machine is being fitted with a sealed reservoir of liquid taken from vials delivered by the Russian, and the operation is guarded far beyond anything a computer factory would need. Alex realises that the gift to Britain's schools is the delivery system for something else, and that his uncle died a few days after reaching the same conclusion.

Alex is caught in the mine and dropped into Sayle's jellyfish tank to die; he cuts his way out through the glass and survives. Sayle, now certain of who he is, explains everything with the pleasure of a man who has waited decades to be understood. The vials hold a modified smallpox virus, and every Stormbreaker in every school will release it at the moment the Prime Minister activates the network. His motive is not money but revenge: sent to an English boarding school as a boy, he was tormented there by the classmate who grew up to become Prime Minister, and he intends to kill the country's children in front of him. Alex escapes the estate with the plant's security behind him and no way to warn anyone in time, because MI6's own people are waiting for a signal that will never come. The launch is hours away.

Alex gets aboard an aircraft bound for London and drops from it into the Science Museum, crashing through the glass roof onto the display below and stopping the Prime Minister with seconds to spare. The network is never switched on and the virus is never released. Sayle runs, is cornered on a rooftop, and turns his gun on Alex; he is shot dead first by Yassen Gregorovich, firing from a helicopter to keep his employers' involvement quiet. Yassen spares Alex, tells him to go home, and promises they will meet again. Afterwards Alex learns that Yassen was the man who killed Ian Rider, and that the people who supplied the virus have not been touched at all. MI6 send him back to Brookland with their thanks and no undertaking to leave him alone, having established that a fourteen-year-old makes an extremely effective agent.

characters.description: The sardonic narrator, an unsuccessful novelist and reluctant chair of the English department at a financially troubled college in Railton, Pennsylvania. He manages colleagues' feuds by provocation, delay, and jokes, even as rumors of layoffs force him to act. His famous father's long absence and his own fear of becoming like him complicate nearly every part of his life.
characters.name: William Henry Devereaux Jr.

characters.description: Hank's capable, clear-sighted wife, who works in education and has spent years translating his evasions into ordinary family life. She loves him without indulging every performance, and her possible move for a better job makes Hank face how much stability in their marriage has depended on her.
characters.name: Lily Devereaux

characters.description: Hank's adult daughter. Her troubled marriage repeatedly pulls her parents into arguments about money, loyalty, and how much help they should offer.
characters.name: Julie Devereaux

characters.description: Julie's husband, whose unreliable choices and tense relationship with Hank make him a recurring point of conflict in the Devereaux family.
characters.name: Russell

characters.description: A senior administrator at the college who warns Hank that budget cuts may require dismissals. He expects the department chair to impose order on a faculty that has made agreement almost impossible.
characters.name: Jacob Rose

characters.description: One of Hank's closest friends on the faculty. He understands the department's absurd rivalries and Hank's habits well enough to offer both companionship and unwelcome accuracy.
characters.name: Tony Coniglia

characters.description: A younger member of the department whose professional insecurity and personal closeness to Hank feed campus gossip at the worst possible time.
characters.name: Meg Quigley

characters.description: A combative English professor and departmental colleague. Like several members of the faculty, he treats the threatened budget cuts as both an institutional emergency and another weapon in old internal battles.
characters.name: Teddy Barnes

characters.description: Hank's father, a nationally prominent literary scholar whose career and abandonment of the family have overshadowed Hank since childhood. News that he may return forces Hank to reconsider grievances he has made central to his identity.
characters.name: William Henry Devereaux Sr.

characters.description: Hank's mother, who built a life after her husband left and has her own reasons for allowing him back into it. Her decision unsettles Hank's familiar account of their family history.
characters.name: Hank's Mother

recaps.ending: The feared purge of the English department does not occur, and the list around which the faculty has organized its panic loses its power. Hank's public threat against the campus geese proves less consequential than the private crises it helped him avoid. His alarming urinary symptoms culminate in passing a kidney stone, giving a concrete answer to an anxiety he had converted into thoughts of mortality and decline. Lily returns, and their marriage survives the week's suspicions, distance, and Hank's resistance to speaking plainly. Hank also has to accept that his father's return and his mother's response belong to them, not to the grievance he has preserved since childhood. The college remains flawed and the department quarrelsome, but Hank ends the week with his family and job intact and with fewer excuses for treating detachment as wisdom.
recaps.in_short: William Henry Devereaux Jr., known as Hank, chairs the English department at an underfunded Pennsylvania college while avoiding nearly every form of authority the job requires. Rumored staff cuts turn his colleagues' rivalries into panic, and his mocking response escalates until he threatens on television to kill a campus goose each day unless the budget is restored. At home, his wife Lily considers a career move, their daughter's marriage is unstable, and news of Hank's famous, long-absent father returning reopens old resentment. Hank also fears that difficulty urinating signals serious illness. His jokes, flirtations, and evasions strain his marriage and friendships while doing little to settle the departmental crisis. The threatened mass dismissals do not happen, his medical terror proves to be a kidney stone, Lily returns, and his parents make their own choices. Hank finishes the chaotic week still at the same imperfect college, but less able to hide from adulthood behind irony.

recaps.text: Hank Devereaux, novelist and temporary chair of the English department at a small Pennsylvania college, introduces a workplace sustained by old grudges, weak budgets, and constant maneuvering. A faculty argument becomes physical enough to injure his nose, establishing how quickly academic disagreements turn personal. At home, Lily recognizes that Hank enjoys provoking crises more than resolving them. Their daughter Julie's marital problems add another demand he would rather meet with commentary than direct help. Hank also begins having trouble urinating, a symptom he conceals while imagining increasingly serious explanations.

The administration signals that serious cuts are coming, and the English faculty expects Hank to protect them while each member privately calculates who should be sacrificed. Meetings collapse into factional arguments. Hank resists providing the certainty everyone demands because he has little real information and distrusts the authority he has been given. His friendships inside the department are strained by the suspicion that he may already possess a dismissal list. Meanwhile, Julie and Russell's troubles draw Lily into practical support and Hank into further conflict with his son-in-law.

Hank learns that his distinguished father may return after years away, reviving anger about the childhood and marriage he abandoned. Hank's mother does not respond according to the role Hank has assigned her in that history, which makes the news harder for him to manage. Lily is considering a professional opportunity that could take her away from Railton, and Hank treats the possibility as both a threat and something he need not discuss honestly. Campus gossip about his closeness to Meg further weakens Lily's trust. His urinary problem persists, linking the week's institutional anxieties to a private fear that his body is failing.

Pressed for a response to the budget crisis, Hank turns protest into spectacle. On camera and near the campus pond, he threatens to kill a goose for every day the administration fails to settle the department's funding. The performance makes him briefly useful to television news and notorious around campus, but it does not give him control of the layoff process. Colleagues interpret everything he does as evidence that he either has a secret list or is protecting selected allies. Lily's absence forces Hank to confront the possibility that his marriage cannot endlessly absorb his flirtations, jokes, and refusal to make clear commitments.

The department's panic peaks as rumors harden into assumed facts. Hank moves between administrators, faculty rivals, his daughter's household, and his parents without finding the clean confrontation he has imagined. His father's return does not provide a satisfying reckoning; instead it reveals that Hank's mother has agency and desires independent of her son's protective story about her. Hank's physical pain becomes impossible to dismiss, while the goose episode and suspicion surrounding Meg leave him with less room to present his behavior as harmless comedy.

The mass dismissal feared by the English department does not materialize, leaving its members to continue together after exposing how readily they turned on one another. Hank's health scare resolves when he passes a kidney stone rather than receiving the catastrophic diagnosis he feared. Lily returns, and the marriage survives, though Hank has been made to see how much he depends on her patience and steadiness. He cannot control his parents' renewed relationship or reduce his father's return to a final judgment on the past. By week's end, the college, the family, and Hank himself remain imperfect but intact; the change is that his usual ironic distance no longer looks like an adequate answer to any of them.

characters.description: A reserved London lawyer known for loyalty and discretion. Though outwardly severe and undemonstrative, he is patient with other people's failings. His concern about an old friend's alarming will draws him into the mystery surrounding Edward Hyde.
characters.name: Mr Gabriel John Utterson

characters.description: Utterson's distant relative and regular walking companion. During one of their Sunday walks, he tells Utterson about seeing a disturbing man knock down and trample a child before producing compensation linked to a highly respectable gentleman.
characters.name: Mr Richard Enfield

characters.description: A small, unsettling man who inspires immediate dislike even in observers unable to identify anything plainly abnormal in his appearance. Enfield sees him cruelly trample a child in the street, after which Hyde uses a key to enter a neglected building and returns with payment bearing another man's name.
characters.name: Mr Edward Hyde

characters.description: A wealthy physician and longtime friend of Utterson. His will leaves everything to Edward Hyde and instructs that Hyde should take his place if Jekyll disappears for an extended period. Known for charitable work and sociability, Jekyll has also pursued private scientific ideas that estranged him from Dr Lanyon.
characters.name: Dr Henry Jekyll

characters.description: A successful physician and an old friend of both Utterson and Jekyll. He has broken with Jekyll over what he regards as unsound and fanciful scientific work, but retains affection for the man he once knew.
characters.name: Dr Lanyon

characters.description: Dr Jekyll's trusted butler. He confirms that Hyde is admitted to the house, has his own key, and is obeyed by the servants under Jekyll's instructions.
characters.name: Poole

characters.description: A courteous and distinguished member of Parliament who carries a letter addressed to Utterson. A maid recognizes him when she witnesses his fatal encounter with Hyde in a London street.
characters.name: Sir Danvers Carew

characters.description: The Scotland Yard officer investigating the murder of Sir Danvers Carew. With Utterson's help, he searches Hyde's Soho rooms and finds evidence connecting Hyde to the killing, but Hyde himself has vanished.
characters.name: Inspector Newcomen

recaps.ending: Lanyon's narrative reveals that Hyde came to him under Jekyll's instructions, mixed a drug from materials retrieved from Jekyll's laboratory, and transformed into Jekyll before his eyes. The experience destroyed Lanyon's health. Jekyll's final statement explains that he created the drug to separate the conflicting sides of his nature and used the form of Hyde to act without the restraints attached to his own identity. Hyde gradually grew stronger, and the changes began occurring without the drug. After Hyde murdered Carew, Jekyll tried to stop transforming, but he could not maintain control. The original potion depended on an unidentified impurity in one chemical, and later supplies would not reproduce it. Trapped in the laboratory and nearly out of the effective mixture, Jekyll wrote his confession while he still could. By the time Utterson and Poole forced entry, Hyde had taken poison and died in Jekyll's clothes. Jekyll was gone, leaving the two identities' shared life ended with Hyde's body.
recaps.in_short: London lawyer Gabriel Utterson investigates the connection between his respectable friend Dr Henry Jekyll and the violent Edward Hyde, whom Jekyll's will names as heir. Hyde murders Sir Danvers Carew and disappears, while Jekyll briefly returns to society before shutting himself inside his laboratory. After Dr Lanyon dies from the shock of a secret encounter and Jekyll's butler fears foul play, Utterson and the servant break into the laboratory and find Hyde dead in Jekyll's clothes. Documents explain that Jekyll invented a potion that transformed him into Hyde, a separate body through which he indulged impulses he wished to conceal. The transformations eventually began without his consent, and the effective drug could not be recreated after its original ingredients ran out. Losing the struggle for control and facing exposure, Hyde kills himself; Jekyll's confession records the end of both identities.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Richard Enfield tells his relative, the lawyer Gabriel Utterson, about a sinister man named Edward Hyde. Enfield once saw Hyde trample a child and then obtain compensation from a neglected building, using a cheque signed by a respected man. The story troubles Utterson because his friend Dr Henry Jekyll has made a will leaving his estate to Hyde and granting Hyde control if Jekyll disappears. Utterson consults Dr Lanyon, another old friend, but learns only that Lanyon and Jekyll have fallen out over Jekyll's unconventional research. After watching the mysterious building, Utterson meets Hyde and finds him immediately repellent. He then visits Jekyll's adjoining house, where the butler Poole confirms that Hyde has a key and the servants have orders to obey him. Utterson fears Hyde is blackmailing Jekyll and may hasten his death to inherit.

At a dinner, Utterson presses Jekyll about the will. Jekyll refuses to explain his relationship with Hyde, insists that he can be free of Hyde whenever he chooses, and asks Utterson to protect Hyde's rights if necessary. Nearly a year later, a maid sees Hyde meet the elderly Sir Danvers Carew in the street. Hyde suddenly attacks Carew with a cane and kills him. A letter found on the victim leads the police to Utterson, who identifies the suspected killer. Utterson accompanies Inspector Newcomen to Hyde's rooms in Soho. Hyde has fled, but the search turns up the broken half of the murder weapon and signs that papers have been burned. The other half of the cane is known to Utterson as a gift he once gave Jekyll, strengthening the unexplained link between the doctor and the fugitive.

Jekyll tells Utterson that his association with Hyde is over and gives him a letter in which Hyde supposedly promises to escape without further help. Utterson's clerk, Mr Guest, notices that Hyde's handwriting closely resembles Jekyll's, though written with a different slant. Utterson concludes that Jekyll forged the letter to shield a murderer. With Hyde absent, Jekyll becomes sociable and resumes his charitable activities, but after several months he abruptly shuts himself away. Lanyon has also changed: visibly ill and terrified, he refuses any further mention of Jekyll and soon dies. He leaves Utterson a sealed account that is to be opened only after Jekyll's death or disappearance. Bound by his professional habits, Utterson does not read it. Jekyll remains secluded, and Poole repeatedly tells callers that the doctor will see no one.

Enfield and Utterson see Jekyll at an upstairs window and begin a friendly conversation with him. A look of terror suddenly crosses Jekyll's face, and he slams the window shut. Later, Poole comes to Utterson in alarm. For days, the person hidden in Jekyll's laboratory has spoken in an unfamiliar voice, kept a masked face from the servants, and sent Poole from chemist to chemist seeking a particular drug. Poole believes his master has been killed and replaced. He and Utterson force their way into the room. Inside they find Hyde dead from poison and wearing clothes made for Jekyll; Jekyll himself is nowhere to be found. A new will names Utterson rather than Hyde as heir. Jekyll has also left instructions directing Utterson first to Lanyon's sealed account and then to Jekyll's own confession, promising an explanation of the locked-room mystery.

Lanyon's account describes receiving urgent instructions from Jekyll to retrieve chemicals and a drawer from the laboratory. Hyde came to collect them, mixed a potion, drank it, and physically changed into Jekyll. The sight shattered Lanyon's health and explains his terror and death. Jekyll's confession then reveals that he developed the drug while trying to divide the opposed elements of his personality. It gave him Hyde's younger, smaller body and allowed him to pursue concealed desires without compromising Jekyll's public identity. As Hyde, he committed escalating acts of violence, culminating in Carew's murder. Jekyll initially believed he could choose between the identities, but Hyde grew stronger and transformations began occurring involuntarily. The effective potion relied on an unknown impurity in the original chemical supply, so replacements failed. Confined to the laboratory and running out of the mixture that restored Jekyll, he completed his statement while expecting Hyde to take permanent control. When Utterson and Poole entered, Hyde used poison to avoid capture and died, bringing Jekyll's life to an end as well.

characters.description: A girl in her early teens, one of the first children raised on a newly settled colony world. She is curious, observant and largely unsupervised outdoors, and she has spent her whole life treating the planet's alien wildlife as neighbors rather than specimens. She looks after her younger brother, keeps her own private map of the countryside around the settlement, and understands the local ecology better than most of the adults do.
characters.name: Cara

characters.description: Cara's much younger brother, a small boy who follows her everywhere and copies whatever she does. He is the person she is responsible for, and the one she is least willing to be careful about losing.
characters.name: Xan

characters.description: Alien machines the colony's children call dogs, roughly the size and shape of large animals, left behind by whatever built the ruins on this world. They move through the countryside without paying attention to people, and they repair things. What they will and will not treat as a thing to be repaired is not something anybody has worked out.
characters.name: The dogs

recaps.ending: Xan is killed in an accident during the military build-up around the settlement. Cara carries his body out to the dogs, and they repair him. What comes back is her brother in every way she can test and not a living boy in any way a doctor could recognize: he does not need to breathe, does not need to eat, and does not heal or fail the way people do. Their parents cannot accept him, and the new authorities on the planet regard him as a specimen and a security problem rather than a child. Cara chooses her brother. The two of them leave the settlement and their family for good and go out into the countryside with the dogs, beyond the reach of anyone who would take Xan apart to find out how he works, and Cara does not intend to remain what she is either. Nobody in the settlement understands what happened, and the world's new owners now know that the alien machines here will rebuild a dead human being. The novella ends there, on a planet that has just become the property of a fleet with no intention of leaving.
recaps.in_short: On a newly settled colony world with alien ruins and machines still running in the countryside, a girl named Cara looks after her small brother Xan and treats the local wildlife as her private responsibility. When a creature she has been feeding is killed, she carries it to the machines the settlement's children call dogs, and they repair it and send it back changed, no longer able to live among its own kind. Then a fleet arrives to claim the planet, the colony is absorbed into a military project it has no say in, and Xan is killed in the disruption. Cara takes her brother to the dogs. They repair him too: he comes back recognizably himself and no longer alive in any way that can be measured, and their parents cannot look at him. Rather than let him be taken, studied or explained, Cara leaves with him, and the two children disappear into the countryside with the machines, changed and beyond recall.

recaps.text: This novella sits in the long gap between the sixth and seventh novels and follows nobody from the main crew. What a listener needs: the ring gates have opened onto more than a thousand habitable worlds, and people have gone through them to settle. Every one of those worlds was built or altered by a civilization that died long ago, and the machinery it left behind is still running in ways nobody understands, sometimes harmlessly and sometimes not. This story takes place on one such planet, among the first generation of colonists and the children they brought with them, and it needs no other background. It does introduce the world and the events that the later novels build on, so a listener working through the series in order will find it sits naturally after the sixth book.

Cara lives with her parents and her small brother Xan in one of the first settlements on a colony world whose native biology behaves in ways nobody has catalogued. She spends her days outdoors, keeps track of a nest of local creatures she has been quietly feeding, and knows the country better than the adults. Among the things running loose out there are alien machines the children call dogs, which wander the landscape ignoring people and repairing whatever they decide is broken. When the creature Cara has been caring for is killed, she takes it to the dogs. They fix it and return it, and it is not right: it comes back alive but altered, and its own kind will not have it. Cara keeps what she has learned to herself.

A fleet arrives to take possession of the planet. The colony, which has been running itself, is absorbed into a military project that nobody consults it about, the countryside fills with equipment and construction, and the rules Cara's family lives under change without discussion. In the middle of that disruption Xan is killed in an accident. Cara knows exactly one thing that can be done about it, and she does it: she carries her brother's body out to the dogs.

The dogs repair Xan. He comes back as himself in every way Cara can test and as nothing a doctor would call alive: he does not breathe, does not eat, and does not injure or heal the way a body does. Their parents cannot accept him, and the planet's new authorities treat him as a specimen and a security problem rather than a child. Cara chooses her brother over her family and over any future in the settlement. The two of them go out into the countryside with the dogs, past the reach of the people who would take Xan apart to learn how he works, and Cara does not intend to stay unchanged herself. The colony is left with a mystery it cannot explain, and the world's new owners are left with the knowledge that the machines here will rebuild a dead human being.

characters.description: A young architect traveling to see his estranged wife, Miriam, in hopes of securing a divorce so he can marry Anne Faulkner. Serious, ambitious, and concerned with acting honorably, he is unsettled by the intrusive stranger who draws him into conversation on the train.
characters.name: Guy Haines

characters.description: A wealthy, idle young man Guy meets during a train journey. Talkative, observant, and already drinking heavily, he quickly presses for intimate details of Guy's life and describes his own hatred of his father. He treats an outrageous idea about exchanging murders as if it were a practical bargain between new friends.
characters.name: Charles Anthony Bruno

characters.description: Guy's estranged wife, who is pregnant by another man but resists giving Guy the uncomplicated divorce he wants. Her changing demands and readiness to interfere with his future make his private frustration easy for Bruno to exploit.
characters.name: Miriam Haines

characters.description: The woman Guy hopes to marry after his divorce. She comes from a secure, affectionate family and believes in Guy's talent and character. Her confidence in their shared future heightens his fear that Bruno's conduct could reach into every part of his life.
characters.name: Anne Faulkner

characters.description: Bruno's indulgent mother, with whom he has an intensely close and childish bond. She excuses his drinking, idleness, and volatility while sharing his taste for luxury and diversion.
characters.name: Mrs. Anthony

characters.description: Bruno's wealthy father. He disapproves of his son's habits and wants him to become responsible, a conflict Bruno interprets as persecution and repeatedly describes in violent terms.
characters.name: Mr. Anthony

characters.description: A private detective retained after Miriam's death. Patient and methodical, he studies the people connected with the case and becomes increasingly interested in the unlikely link between Guy and Bruno.
characters.name: Arthur Gerard

characters.description: Anne's father, a prosperous man whose family welcomes Guy. His trust and social standing represent the stable adult life Guy hopes to enter through his marriage and architectural career.
characters.name: Mr. Faulkner

characters.description: A friend in Guy and Anne's social circle who notices Bruno's excessive interest in Guy. He sees more clearly than most that Bruno's appearances are neither casual nor harmless.
characters.name: Bob Treacher

characters.description: The man with whom Miriam had been involved. Guy eventually seeks him out while trying to speak honestly about the chain of violence that began around Miriam, making him an unintended witness to Guy's need to confess.
characters.name: Owen Markman

recaps.ending: After Guy has built a successful public life with Anne, Bruno remains a dangerous reminder of the two murders binding them together. Gerard reconstructs their connection and keeps searching for proof. During a sailing trip, an intoxicated Bruno falls overboard; Guy tries to save him, but Bruno drowns. His death removes the threat of direct exposure without freeing Guy from his own guilt. Guy visits Owen Markman, Miriam's former lover, and confesses the exchange: Bruno killed Miriam, and Guy later killed Bruno's father. Owen responds with unexpected sympathy, but Gerard has followed Guy and hears enough to complete his case. The novel closes with Guy facing arrest, his effort to preserve an honorable identity finally undone by the confession he could no longer suppress.
recaps.in_short: Architect Guy Haines meets wealthy Charles Bruno on a train and is drawn into a conversation about the people obstructing their lives. Bruno proposes that they exchange murders, eliminating motive: he will kill Guy's estranged wife, Miriam, if Guy kills Bruno's hated father. Guy rejects the idea, but Bruno murders Miriam and then insists that Guy owes him his half of the bargain. Harassed and afraid that suspicion will destroy his career and marriage to Anne Faulkner, Guy eventually kills Mr. Anthony. The shared crimes do not produce freedom. Bruno becomes increasingly possessive and conspicuous, while detective Arthur Gerard traces the connection between the men. Bruno later drowns despite Guy's attempt to rescue him. Still unable to live with what he has done, Guy confesses to Miriam's former lover, unaware that Gerard is listening. He is exposed and faces arrest.

recaps.text: Architect Guy Haines is traveling to Metcalf to discuss a divorce with his estranged wife, Miriam, so that he can marry Anne Faulkner. On the train he meets Charles Bruno, a wealthy young stranger who drinks heavily and draws Guy into an unusually personal conversation. After learning that Miriam is delaying Guy's plans and that Guy resents her, Bruno explains his own hatred of his father. He proposes a pair of unconnected killings: Bruno could murder Miriam, while Guy could kill Bruno's father. With no ordinary motive linking either killer to the victim, Bruno believes both crimes would be safe. Guy refuses and tries to dismiss the proposal as drunken fantasy, but Bruno has learned his name, destination, and circumstances and behaves as though an agreement has been made.

Guy's meeting with Miriam confirms that she will not give him a simple release. Meanwhile, Bruno travels to Metcalf and follows her to an amusement park, acting on the plan Guy rejected. He strangles Miriam and leaves without an obvious connection to her. News of her death brings Guy the freedom he wanted while immediately filling him with dread: he understands who killed her and why. Bruno contacts Guy as if he has performed a service between partners. Guy cannot report him without revealing the train conversation and inviting suspicion that he requested the murder, so his silence gives Bruno the leverage to demand that the exchange be completed.

Bruno repeatedly telephones and writes to Guy, insisting that Guy kill Mr. Anthony. Guy attempts to ignore him and concentrates on Anne and a major architectural commission, but Bruno treats every refusal as delay rather than rejection. He enters Guy's social world and threatens to make their association visible. Detective Arthur Gerard begins examining Miriam's death and takes an interest in its surrounding relationships. Guy remains trapped between exposure and complicity: telling the truth could make him look like the author of the crime, while continued silence allows Bruno to invade his work, friendships, and future marriage.

Exhausted by Bruno's pressure and afraid that the truth about Miriam will destroy his life with Anne, Guy gives in to the bargain. He studies the Anthony home and goes there at night, trying to treat the act as a task imposed from outside himself. He enters the house and kills Bruno's father, then escapes. The second murder appears to complete the exchange, but it leaves Guy psychologically bound to Bruno rather than rid of him. Bruno is exhilarated by their shared secret and assumes an intimacy Guy cannot accept, while Guy returns to Anne carrying guilt that cannot be reconciled with the respectable identity he is building.

Guy marries Anne and his architectural career advances, yet Bruno continues to appear, drink, and speak with dangerous familiarity. His attachment to Guy grows more possessive now that each man has killed for the other. People around Guy notice the unwanted connection, and Anne senses that her husband is withholding something profound. Gerard compares the circumstances of the two murders and investigates how Guy and Bruno could have met. The plan's supposed strength—the absence of a conventional motive—weakens as Bruno makes the relationship between them increasingly visible. Guy tries to protect Anne and his career while recognizing that Bruno's instability may expose them both.

Gerard closes in on the history linking Guy and Bruno. During a sailing trip, the intoxicated Bruno falls into the water. Guy attempts to rescue him, but Bruno drowns, ending the immediate danger that he will deliberately reveal their bargain. His death does not end Guy's guilt. Unable to sustain his divided life, Guy seeks out Owen Markman, the man formerly involved with Miriam, and tells him the truth: Bruno murdered Miriam after their meeting on the train, and Guy later fulfilled the exchange by killing Bruno's father. Owen does not react with the condemnation Guy expects. Gerard, however, has followed Guy and overhears the confession. With the investigator finally holding the connection and admission he needs, Guy's respectable life collapses and he faces arrest for the crime he committed.

characters.description: A dark elf ranger who left his people's underground city years ago and has made a home in Icewind Dale, fighting with two scimitars and a summoned panther. He is going south with Bruenor partly out of loyalty and partly because he has never seen the wider world, and he knows that every settled place they pass through will treat him as a monster before it treats him as anything else.
characters.name: Drizzt Do'Urden

characters.description: A dwarf king and master smith from Icewind Dale, driven out of his clan's ancestral home as a boy and set on finding it again. What he has to go on is a child's memories: a valley, a mountain with four peaks, and streams that ran silver. He is stubborn to the point of recklessness about it and short with anyone who suggests the search is hopeless.
characters.name: Bruenor Battlehammer

characters.description: A young barbarian of Icewind Dale, enormous and immensely strong, who carries the warhammer Aegis-fang that Bruenor forged for him. His five years of service to the dwarf are over and he is now king of the tundra tribes, but he has chosen to spend this season repaying a debt he no longer owes. Away from the only country he knows, his certainties get tested constantly.
characters.name: Wulfgar

characters.description: A halfling from the southern city of Calimport who has spent years in Icewind Dale being as comfortable and as useless as possible. He carries a ruby pendant, stolen from the thieves' guild he fled, whose enchantment makes anyone who studies it inclined to agree with him. He is on this road mainly because staying still had become the more dangerous option.
characters.name: Regis

characters.description: A great black panther summoned from another world by an onyx figurine Drizzt carries, able to stay for a limited time before she must return and rest.
characters.name: Guenhwyvar

characters.description: A young human woman raised by Bruenor as his daughter among the dwarves of Icewind Dale. Capable, level-headed and a better shot than anyone gives her credit for, she is left behind when the company sets out and is not happy about it.
characters.name: Catti-brie

characters.description: The master of a powerful thieves' guild in the southern city of Calimport, wealthy, unhurried and vindictive on a long timescale. He has spent years hunting the halfling who robbed him, and he wants the stolen pendant back rather more than he wants revenge, though he intends to have both.
characters.name: Pasha Pook

characters.description: An assassin of extraordinary skill, sent north from Calimport to bring back a thief and a stolen gem. He is precise, patient and entirely without appetite for anything except the work itself and the question of whether anyone alive can match him. He fights with a saber and a jeweled dagger.
characters.name: Artemis Entreri

characters.description: A wizard of the Hosttower of the Arcane in the port city of Luskan, cautious, manipulative and consumed by his own standing among his rivals. He has been trying for years to learn what really destroyed the invading army in Icewind Dale, and he believes the dark elf travelling south can tell him.
characters.name: Dendybar the Mottled

characters.description: Dendybar's apprentice, an ambitious young mage who does the practical work her master will not leave his tower for. She is competent, careful and clear-eyed about the fact that her advancement depends entirely on bringing back results.
characters.name: Sydney

characters.description: A soldier of Luskan's city guard who reports privately to Dendybar and hopes the arrangement will lift him out of the ranks. He is the one who first spots the travellers from the north.
characters.name: Jierdan

characters.description: A golem in Dendybar's service, a manufactured thing of enormous strength that follows one order at a time and does not stop. It can be set on a trail and will keep to it regardless of terrain, obstacles or losses.
characters.name: Bok

characters.description: A wizard of Longsaddle, a member of an eccentric family of mages whose home is a running experiment in what magic will tolerate. Enthusiastic, absent-minded and genuinely well meaning, he attaches himself to the company's quest with more excitement than judgement.
characters.name: Harkle Harpell

characters.description: The ruler of Silverymoon, a city on the River Rauvin known for its learning and its tolerance, and one of the most powerful figures in the north. She is courteous, formidable and interested in the company's quest for reasons of her own, and she treats the dark elf with a plain civility he has met almost nowhere else.
characters.name: Lady Alustriel

characters.description: A dragon of shadow that has lain in the deepest mines beneath the dwarven halls since the clan that dug them was driven out. It is old, black as a hole in the air, and the reason the current occupants of the halls hold them without dispute.
characters.name: Shimmergloom

recaps.ending: Driven toward Garumn's Gorge with the gray dwarves behind them, the companions try to cross the bridge and get out of the mountain. Shimmergloom comes up out of the chasm to stop them. Bruenor soaks himself in oil, sets himself alight and leaps onto the shadow dragon's back, and the two of them fall together into the gorge; the fight and the collapse that follows give the others the seconds they need to get clear. Sydney is killed and Dendybar's expedition destroyed with her, and the wizard himself does not survive the failure. In the confusion Entreri takes Regis and starts south for Calimport, making no secret of his route, because what he wants now is for the dark elf to follow him. Drizzt, Wulfgar and Catti-brie escape the mountain with nothing: Mithril Hall is found and still held by its occupiers, Bruenor is gone into a chasm no one could survive, and the friend they came out of Icewind Dale with is in an assassin's hands. Having nothing they can do for Bruenor, they turn south to do the one thing left, and set out for Calimport to take Regis back.
recaps.in_short: Bruenor Battlehammer leads Drizzt, Wulfgar and Regis out of Icewind Dale to find Mithril Hall, the ancestral home of his clan, guided by nothing but childhood memories. Behind them, the assassin Artemis Entreri comes north for Regis and the stolen ruby pendant, taking Bruenor's daughter Catti-brie prisoner to follow the trail, and the Luskan wizard Dendybar sets his apprentice Sydney and a golem after the company to learn what Drizzt knows. The road takes the friends through hostile Luskan, the eccentric wizards of Longsaddle, a meeting outside Silverymoon with Lady Alustriel that finally gives Bruenor his bearings, and the troll-ridden Evermoors. They find Mithril Hall held by gray dwarves in the service of Shimmergloom, a shadow dragon. Cornered at Garumn's Gorge, Bruenor sets himself alight, leaps onto the dragon and falls with it into the chasm so the others can escape. Sydney dies and the wizard's expedition is destroyed. Entreri seizes Regis in the chaos and starts south for Calimport, and Drizzt, Wulfgar and Catti-brie follow him.

recaps.text: Previously: in Icewind Dale, the dark elf ranger Drizzt Do'Urden, the dwarf king Bruenor Battlehammer, the halfling Regis and the young barbarian Wulfgar helped break the invasion of the wizard Akar Kessell, whose army was destroyed and who died buried beneath an avalanche along with the artifact that had made him. Wulfgar had come to Bruenor as a captive after an earlier barbarian raid and served five years, learning the forge from the dwarf and swordplay from Drizzt; Bruenor forged him the warhammer Aegis-fang, and by the war's end he was king of the tundra tribes. Bruenor, dug out of his own collapsed tunnels and expecting to die of it, told Drizzt about Mithril Hall, the lost ancestral home of Clan Battlehammer, from which his people were driven when he was a boy and whose location he cannot remember. He recovered and held himself to the search. Regis, who fled a thieves' guild in the southern city of Calimport years ago with a stolen ruby pendant, has learned that his old master has finally traced him, and prefers the road to waiting.

The four leave Ten-Towns in spring, heading south and west with almost nothing to navigate by: Bruenor recalls a valley, a mountain of four peaks and streams that ran silver, and no map in the north matches the description. Catti-brie stays behind in Icewind Dale. In Calimport, Pasha Pook loses patience with years of fruitless searching and sends his best assassin, Artemis Entreri, to bring back both the pendant and the halfling who took it. Entreri reaches Icewind Dale, works out who Regis was travelling with, and takes Catti-brie prisoner to use as a guide and a hostage, following the company's trail south.

The company reaches the port city of Luskan, where a dwarf, a barbarian, a halfling and a hooded figure attract exactly the attention they hoped to avoid. Dendybar the Mottled, a wizard of the Hosttower of the Arcane, has been trying for years to learn what actually destroyed Kessell's army, and when his informant Jierdan reports a dark elf in the city he sends his apprentice Sydney to take Drizzt alive. The attempt fails and the friends get out of Luskan, but the pursuit is now organized: Sydney continues south with the golem Bok on the trail, and Entreri, who cares nothing for the wizard's questions but a great deal about the tracking, attaches himself to the hunt.

At Longsaddle the company is taken in by the Harpells, a family of wizards whose hospitality is more dangerous than most ambushes, and Harkle Harpell decides the quest is exactly what he has been waiting for. At Silverymoon, Drizzt is turned away at the gates for being what he is, and Lady Alustriel comes out to meet him beyond the walls instead, treating him with a plain courtesy that unsettles him more than the refusal did. She gives Bruenor what the whole journey has lacked: a name and a direction, pointing him toward the Evermoors and the mountain called Fourthpeak. The friends turn east with a destination for the first time.

The road east is the worst of the journey. The town of Nesme, which lives on the edge of the troll country, meets them with open hostility and drives them off, and they cross the Evermoors under near-constant attack, fighting trolls and worse in country that heals its monsters faster than they can be killed. They fight through a pass held by orcs. Behind them Entreri, Sydney and the golem close the gap steadily, since Bok does not need to rest and Entreri does not choose to. Bruenor begins to recognize the shape of the land from his childhood, and finds the concealed door in the mountainside that opens onto Mithril Hall.

Inside, Mithril Hall is not empty. Gray dwarves hold the halls and the forges in the service of Shimmergloom, a shadow dragon that has lain in the mines beneath since Clan Battlehammer was driven out. Bruenor walks through the rooms of his childhood, finds the relics of his father's reign and takes up his family's arms, and the reunion with his past is short: the duergar discover the intruders and the halls fill with pursuit. Entreri's party gets inside the complex as well, and in the confusion Catti-brie breaks free of the assassin and finds her father and her friends, joining the running fight through the tunnels.

Pushed back toward Garumn's Gorge, the companions try to cross the bridge and escape the mountain, and Shimmergloom rises out of the chasm to cut them off. Bruenor douses himself in oil, sets himself alight and throws himself onto the dragon's back; the two fall together into the gorge, and the collapse that follows buys the others their way out. Sydney is killed and Dendybar's expedition destroyed with her. Entreri seizes Regis during the escape and starts south for Calimport, making his route obvious because he wants Drizzt to follow. Drizzt, Wulfgar and Catti-brie get clear of the mountain having found Mithril Hall and lost everything else: the halls still held, Bruenor gone into the gorge, Regis in an assassin's hands. With nothing they can do for Bruenor, they turn south after Entreri.

characters.description: A resourceful boy growing up in extreme poverty in Victorian London. Fiercely attached to his mother and sisters, Jim tries to keep his family together after eviction and then struggles to preserve his freedom through the workhouse, the streets, and forced labor. His experiences eventually bring the plight of homeless children to Dr Barnardo's attention.
characters.name: Jim Jarvis
